title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) measuring whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the fraction of validator‑passing vendor‑specific CLI configurations produced from operator intent, relative to direct LLM generation. Tasks were a curated multi‑vendor (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) intent manifest; a deterministic validator encoded syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic routing‑reachability, and destructive‑pattern checks; and the declared model snapshot was gpt-5-mini. Under the preregistered paired design (shared initial candidate per task), every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 300/300, guarded = 300/300; n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). Because the guarded arm invoked zero repair calls, the preregistered single‑repair policy was not exercised and no repair‑success diagnostics are observed. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the 300‑task manifest, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being proposed for intent→configuration translation in NetOps. Operators commonly mitigate risk with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops. We evaluated the operational benefit of a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) intervention by preregistering a confirmatory paired test: for each task generate a single initial candidate (shared across arms); the baseline succeeds if the validator accepts that candidate; the guarded arm also permits one deterministic automatic repair if the initial candidate fails. Our preregistered objective (study_id study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e) was to test whether the guarded policy increases the per‑task probability of producing a validator‑passing configuration.
sections.related_work: We situate this study amid recent work on LLM→configuration, validator‑guided generation, and generate‑validate architectures. Representative verified sources used for positioning include intent‑driven NetOps proposals and configuration verification literature: Nguyen et al. (2024) on intent→configuration; Chakraborty et al. (2024) and Mondal et al. (2025) on LLM‑based configuration automation; Weitz et al. (2016) on SMT‑based BGP policy verification; and NetLLMBench (2024) as a recent benchmark effort. These verified works motivate focusing on validator‑centered reliability rather than raw language accuracy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The experimental plan was preregistered (study_id study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6) and frozen prior to execution. Design: paired binary outcomes for n=300 tasks. For each task one initial candidate (shared) was generated; baseline outcome = validator(initial_candidate); guarded outcome = validator(initial_candidate) OR validator(repair_candidate) where a single automatic repair call is allowed if the validator rejects the initial candidate. Task manifest and validator: the curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest and per‑task payloads (intent, initial_state, required_sequence, difficulty) are published (artifact: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The deterministic validator used in scoring is referenced as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0); validator traces are embedded in execution/scoring/*.json (representative examples are cited below). Model and prompts: declared model snapshot gpt-5-mini; model configuration and prompt/transformation metadata are published (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa; execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 = ef4f9a7e6e5e67398eca449221f29490ff0a107c38e2fd07cf833f9c35e4971a). Execution contract: shared initial generation only (one model call per task), repair budget ≤1 call per task in guarded arm. All raw outputs, provider traces, scoring traces, and hashes were recorded and published.

sections.discussion: Interpretation. The run produced a ceiling outcome: the declared model snapshot and prompt regime generated initial candidates that satisfied the deterministic validator for every curated task; consequently the bounded guarded policy could not change outcomes and produced a null paired difference. Statistical note on degenerate contingency tables: when n10=n01=0 (no discordant pairs) the exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p=1.00 and bootstrap percentile CIs for the paired difference collapse to the observed point estimate; this behavior reflects that the observed data contain no discordant information to support a nonzero paired effect. Operational implication. The absence of measurable guarded benefit here does not imply G‑V‑R is unnecessary in general. A measurable safety benefit requires a nonzero initial failure rate (for the chosen generator/prompt/model snapshot) or a validator of broader coverage (dynamic/emulation checks, deeper routing semantics) that the generator is prone to violate. Recommendations: (1) instrument initial failure rates in real deployments; (2) align validator fidelity with operational harms of interest; (3) select repair budgets after measuring failure severity and empirical repairability. Reproducible follow‑ups should (a) increase task hardness (adversarial/OOD tasks), (b) expand validator scope (simulation/emulation), (c) test multiple model families and snapshots, and (d) permit iterative repair policies.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded G‑V‑R policy on a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest. Under the declared model snapshot, prompt regime, and deterministic validator, every initial candidate passed the validator and the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked; hence no marginal improvement was observed. The operational value of G‑V‑R depends on generator error rate, validator coverage, and task hardness. All run artifacts (task manifest, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, analysis artifacts) are published and hash‑signed for reproducible follow‑ups.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, forbidden destructive patterns) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
